sys-workflows-basics.title: What an AI Workflow really is — in plain terms
sys-workflows-basics.what:
A workflow is a chain of steps: something comes in → AI processes it → result is checked → passed on. For example: email arrives → AI reads → classifies type → drafts reply → human reviews → sent.

This is NOT a single chat prompt. And NOT just "trigger-based automation". The simplest form — [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]] (A → B → C). A workflow is when you have "input → AI → output" that works the same way every day.
sys-workflows-basics.why:
When you work with AI in chat — you re-explain context every time. That's fine for a one-off. But if you do the same thing 50 times a week — you need a workflow: configure once → it repeats.

A workflow turns "AI helps me" into "I have a process, AI is part of it".
sys-workflows-basics.when:
When the task repeats more than 3 times a week.

When you notice:
- "I'm writing this same prompt again"
- "I'm copying data back and forth again"
- 5 people on the team do the same thing — each in their own way
- Quality depends on mood and tiredness
sys-workflows-basics.impact:
Before: every morning 1 hour sorting email. After: AI sorted it overnight, you spend 10 minutes checking.

Main point isn't "faster", it's "predictable". Workflow gives stable quality: 9 out of 10 times the result is good, you know what to expect.
sys-workflows-basics.example:
Workflow "prepare for a customer meeting":
1. In the morning AI checks your calendar
2. For each meeting it finds the customer profile in the CRM
3. Pulls the latest email thread
4. Writes a brief summary: "yesterday discussed X, open items Y, pain points Z"
5. By 8:00 your Slack has summaries for all meetings of the day

You walk into the meeting prepared, not "hold on, let me remember".
sys-workflows-basics.mistakes:
Main mistake: try to build a "universal workflow for everything". You'll end up with a monster nobody understands.

Better: 5 simple workflows for specific tasks. Each does one thing well.

Second mistake: automating a step that requires human judgement. If AI decides "should I send this to the client" — sooner or later it'll send something inappropriate.

sys-linear-chain.title: Linear Chain — a simple sequence of steps
sys-linear-chain.what:
The simplest kind of workflow: A → B → C. Each step takes the output of the previous one. No branches, no "if-then". Just a straight line.

Sounds primitive, but 80% of real AI tasks look exactly like this. No need to overcomplicate upfront.
sys-linear-chain.why:
A simple chain is easy to fix. If something goes wrong — you can see at which step it broke. You add complex branching only when you really can't do without it.

Rule: start with a linear chain. If it covers 80% of cases — leave it. Add complexity when you hit a wall.
sys-linear-chain.when:
When the task splits into clear sequential steps. One step — one meaning.

Examples:
- Transcribe audio → extract decisions → send to Notion
- Receive an article → translate → check terminology → publish
- Read a resume → extract skills → match to job → score
sys-linear-chain.impact:
Linear chain works 9 times out of 10. When it breaks — you can tell where (you see which step failed).

Complex branching workflows work 6 times out of 10, and it's unclear what to fix.

Simplicity = reliability.
sys-linear-chain.example:
Workflow "onboard a new customer":
1. Manager fills out a form with basic customer info
2. AI generates a personalized welcome email
3. AI creates an onboarding checklist tailored to their industry
4. AI drafts a contract with the right pricing
5. Manager checks everything → sends

Each step is simple. If AI got step 3 wrong — manager sees "wrong industry in checklist" → fixes it → moves on. To stop errors reaching the client — put a [[node:sys-quality-gates|Quality Gate]] before sending. No need to redo everything.
sys-linear-chain.mistakes:
Main mistake: add branching from the start ("if enterprise, ..., if SMB, ..."). Result: a workflow nobody understands, impossible to maintain.

Better: build 2 separate linear chains — one for enterprise, one for SMB. Simpler and clearer.

Second mistake: bundling 3 actions into one step ("read the document, summarize, translate to English"). Split them — debugging is 10× easier.

sys-quality-gates.title: Quality Gates — check before passing it on
sys-quality-gates.what:
A point between workflow steps where the result is checked before going further. Either AI checks it (by rules), or a human does.

Without checks, errors pile up. AI got step 1 wrong → step 2 gets garbage → step 3 confidently sends nonsense to a client. (Related: [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation to a human]] when a gate fails.)
sys-quality-gates.why:
AI gets things wrong 5-15% of the time. That's fine. What's not fine — letting errors slip down the chain.

A gate catches mistakes early, when they're cheap. Fix at step 2 = 1 minute. Explaining to a client later = a week of damage.
sys-quality-gates.when:
Anywhere an error is costly:
- Before sending to a client
- Before writing to a database
- Before charging money
- Before publishing on social media
- Before passing to a lawyer

Where "we can redo it" — gates aren't needed.
sys-quality-gates.impact:
Without gates: 1 in 10 results goes to a client with an error. Once a month — a major incident.

With gates: 1 in 100 errors slip through. No major incidents — caught either by AI rule-check or by a human.

Main point: you can relax about running AI on real tasks.
sys-quality-gates.example:
Workflow "send a contract to a customer":
1. AI generates the contract from template + customer data
2. **Gate 1 (AI):** check that all required fields are filled, amounts match the CRM, no duplicate paragraphs
3. If the gate failed → return to step 1 with a note on what to fix
4. **Gate 2 (human):** lawyer scans for 30 seconds → ok / not ok
5. If both gates pass → send

Result: 95% of contracts go without lawyer involvement. The lawyer only spends time on edge cases. Zero number errors.
sys-quality-gates.mistakes:
Main mistake: a gate at every step. The workflow becomes "AI works 10 seconds → human reviews 5 minutes → AI works 10 seconds → human reviews...". Nobody will stand it.

Better: gate only before actions with consequences (send, write, charge).

Second mistake: "AI checks AI" as a gate. If the main model made a mistake — the checking model will make the same one. You need either a different check principle (rules, not AI) or a human.

sys-rag-architecture.title: RAG — how AI fetches the right document from your base
sys-rag-architecture.what:
You know how Google searches websites? RAG is the same search, but over your documents, plus an AI that assembles an answer from what it found.

The word RAG sounds scary, but the idea is simple: 1) user asks, 2) the system finds 3-5 relevant chunks from the base, 3) AI composes an answer with citations.
sys-rag-architecture.why:
Without RAG, AI can only do what it learned in training. Ask about your company — it gives generic answers or makes things up.

With RAG — AI answers "here's the doc from March 14th, here's what it says, here's the link". Stops making things up, starts citing.
sys-rag-architecture.when:
When AI should answer based on your documents:
- Company knowledge base
- Internal policies
- Product documentation
- Customer conversation history
- Any data not on the public internet (see [[node:ai-data-systems|AI Data Systems]] for the big picture)

If AI can answer from general knowledge — RAG isn't needed.
sys-rag-architecture.impact:
Simple RAG (fetch — feed to AI): works well on 50-60% of queries.

RAG with relevance checks on what's found: 75-85%.

RAG with clarifying questions and re-ranking: 90%+.

Main point: users stop getting "sorry, I don't know" on questions whose answers are in the docs.
sys-rag-architecture.example:
SaaS product support:
1. Customer writes: "how do I export a report with a region filter for the quarter?"
2. RAG searches product docs — finds 3 relevant sections
3. AI assembles the answer: "Go to Reports → Export. Pick the Region filter, period Custom → set the quarter. Details: link to docs. If Region filter is disabled — you're on Starter plan, upgrade here."
4. Customer gets a concrete answer with links in 5 seconds instead of waiting for an agent

Self-service conversion: from 20% to 70%.
sys-rag-architecture.mistakes:
Main mistake: dumping everything into the base — old drafts, duplicates, outdated policies. AI finds noise and confidently cites a 2019 doc.

Better: fewer documents, but current ones. Set up a process for removing the outdated.

Second mistake: not showing sources. If AI answers without a link to "where it got it" — nobody trusts it, everyone goes to a human anyway.

sys-context-passing.title: How to pass context between steps
sys-context-passing.what:
In a multi-step workflow (see [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]] and [[node:sys-workflows-basics|workflow basics]]) there's a question: what exactly do you pass to the next AI step? Everything that came before? Only the important part? A compressed summary?

Three options:
1. **Pass everything** — simple, but expensive and slow
2. **Pass only what's needed** — but you have to decide what's needed
3. **Compress into a summary** — AI compresses, then passes
sys-context-passing.why:
If you pass everything — at step 5 your input is 100 pages of history. AI reads for 30 seconds, costs as much as a coffee, sometimes doesn't even fit the limit.

If you pass too little — the next step loses context and asks "who is this anyway?".

The right choice depends on the task.
sys-context-passing.when:
Pass EVERYTHING — when there are 2-3 steps and context is small.

Pass ONLY WHAT'S NEEDED — when you have a clear understanding of what each step needs (e.g. step 3 needs only the customer and their plan, the rest doesn't matter).

Use SUMMARY — when context is large and dynamic (long conversations, multi-step research).
sys-context-passing.impact:
Right context = workflow runs in seconds, costs pennies.

Wrong = workflow costs 10× more than it could, sometimes breaks because the input doesn't fit.

Main point: AI gets only what it needs — answers faster and more accurately.
sys-context-passing.example:
Workflow "process a long customer conversation" (50+ messages):

Bad: every step gets the entire history. Step 5 receives 30k words on input, costs $0.50 per request.

Good:
1. Step 1: AI reads the whole conversation → makes a 200-word summary ("customer complains about X, tried Y, ready for Z")
2. Steps 2-5: receive summary + last 5 messages + customer profile
3. Cost drops 20×. Answer quality goes up (AI isn't drowning in noise).
sys-context-passing.mistakes:
Main mistake: "to be safe let's pass everything". Each step ends up slow and expensive, AI gets distracted by irrelevant stuff.

Second mistake: regenerating the summary every time. If context doesn't change — cache the summary and reuse. Otherwise you pay for the same work 10 times.

sys-multi-agent-patterns.title: Multi-Agent — 4 ways AIs work as a team
sys-multi-agent-patterns.what:
Multi-Agent isn't "throw a few AIs at the task and hope". There are 4 standard ways they work together:

1. **Coordinator-Worker** — boss + executors. Boss splits the task, executors do their part, boss assembles the result.
2. **Debate** — two AIs argue about an answer, a third decides who's right.
3. **Reflection** — one AI does the work, another reviews and gives feedback, the first revises.
4. **Tool-using** — one AI but it can call functions: search the web, run code, query a database.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.why:
Knowing the patterns saves time. Without them you'd reinvent the wheel for every project. With them you say "let's use Reflection here" — the team knows what that means, builds it in a day.

It's like in cooking: knowing "sauté", "simmer", "poach" — you don't explain step by step every time, you just name the technique.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.when:
**Coordinator-Worker** — when the task can be split into independent pieces (e.g. "research 5 competitors" = 5 workers in parallel).

**Debate** — when the answer is non-obvious and you want to check different angles (legal questions, strategic decisions).

**Reflection** — when quality matters and the first try is usually "meh" (writing texts, generating code).

**Tool-using** — when AI needs real data (current weather, database, [[node:cap-search|web search]]). Most common pattern in production.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.impact:
The right pattern = your AI system works predictably, costs are clear, you can debug it.

The wrong pattern = expensive, slow, can't tell why something broke. Like baking a cake on a frying pan: technically possible, in practice — pain.

Main point: pick a known pattern, don't invent your own.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.example:
Customer support tier-1 → tier-2 escalation = Coordinator-Worker pattern:

1. Coordinator AI gets the message, classifies the type (password / billing / bug / complaint)
2. Routes to a specialized worker: password → Worker A (has password reset instructions), billing → Worker B (sees the customer's billing), bug → Worker C (knows current known issues), complaint → human
3. Worker does their part, returns the answer
4. Coordinator wraps it in a nice format and sends to the customer

Result: 4 specialized AIs handle 80% of tickets. Each is simple. You can debug if classification breaks — by looking at the coordinator, not the whole system.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.mistakes:
Main mistake: "let's use all 4 patterns at once". You'll get a system no one understands, including you. Start with one — usually Tool-using or Coordinator-Worker.

Second mistake: Reflection without limits. "AI writes, another AI reviews, the first rewrites, the second reviews again..." — they can loop for hours. Always cap the iterations (max 2-3 rounds).

Third mistake: Debate for simple tasks. Two AIs arguing about "capital of France" = waste of money. Debate only for genuinely non-obvious questions.

sys-escalation-paths.title: When AI calls a human — and how to do it right
sys-escalation-paths.what:
Escalation is the moment AI says "a human is needed here" (big picture — [[node:ai-human-collaboration|AI + Human]]) and hands off. Sounds simple, but the details matter: when it escalates, what it prepares for the human, what happens after.

Bad escalation: "AI couldn't do it, you figure it out". Good escalation: "AI couldn't do this specific thing, I've already gathered context, tried these options, recommend looking here".
sys-escalation-paths.why:
Without escalation, AI either keeps trying the same failing approach (annoying the customer), or gives up on the first hurdle (then why have it at all).

Good escalation = AI does 70% of the work, hands off the hard 30% pre-warmed. The human opens the task and immediately gets it.
sys-escalation-paths.when:
Set explicit escalation rules:
- Customer wrote "complaint" / "cancellation" / "lawsuit"
- AI failed twice in a row
- Deal amount above a threshold
- Task category marked "always human"
- Customer explicitly said "get me a human"
sys-escalation-paths.impact:
Without rules: AI either tortures the customer with endless attempts, or calls a human for every little thing.

With rules: 80% of tasks AI handles itself, 20% go to a human with ready context. Human spends not "an hour figuring it out" but "5 minutes to make a call".

Trust in the system goes up for everyone: customers, agents, management.
sys-escalation-paths.example:
E-commerce support:
1. Customer: "my order didn't arrive"
2. AI checks tracking → stuck at sorting center → writes "order is delayed, expected delivery on such-and-such date"
3. Customer: "this is the third time, I want a full refund"
4. AI detects "refund" + "third time" → escalation
5. AI prepares for the agent: "customer Ivanov, order #1234, 3rd delay in 2 months, previously ordered $50k, status — angry. Recommendation: refund + promo code. Conversation history: link"
6. Agent opens → sees full context → makes a decision in 2 minutes

Customer: gets a live person quickly. Agent: doesn't spend 20 minutes on "tell me again".
sys-escalation-paths.mistakes:
Main mistake: escalate by AI confidence ("if confidence < 80% — call a human"). AI is almost always confident. Either it doesn't escalate at all, or escalates randomly.

Better: escalate by task type and keywords — that's explainable.

Second mistake: passing a "bare" task to the human without context. The agent spends time figuring out what AI already knew. Always prep a summary before handoff.

sys-evals-benchmarks.title: How to actually check that AI works well
sys-evals-benchmarks.what:
Evals aren't "tested on 5 examples and seems ok". It's a set of 50-200 typical tasks you regularly run AI against: quality, accuracy, style.

When you change the prompt or model — you run them and see if it got better or worse. Without guessing.
sys-evals-benchmarks.why:
Without evals you don't know if AI actually works. Might work. Might seem to work. Might work on your examples and break on real users.

With evals you have a number: "80% of answers are good". Changed the prompt — became 85%. Progress is visible.
sys-evals-benchmarks.when:
When AI is out with users. Not "when we need it" — by then it's too late. (Part of [[node:ai-operations|AI Operations]] — production-readiness practices.)

Signals you're missing evals:
- You want to improve a prompt, but don't know if changes helped
- Users complain about quality — you can't tell if it really got worse
- Thinking of switching models — no data to compare
- The team argues "AI works" / "no it doesn't" — no numbers
sys-evals-benchmarks.impact:
Without evals: the team tweaks prompts "by feel". Half of changes make it worse, nobody notices.

With evals: every change is backed by a number. You see what works and what doesn't. Quality grows steadily, not "got lucky sometimes".

Main point: you manage quality instead of praying.
sys-evals-benchmarks.example:
AI assistant for writing B2B sales emails:
1. Collected 100 examples: topic + brief context + expected style
2. Each example has a "gold standard" answer (written by a human or manually validated)
3. Each prompt change is run on these 100 → AI scores similarity to the gold + a human spot-checks
4. You see: "previous version — 72% good answers, new — 81%". Ship the new one.
5. Weekly automatic run → if it drops below 75% (model degradation) → alert

The team sees real progress, not "feels a bit better".
sys-evals-benchmarks.mistakes:
Main mistake: "we'll do evals later". A year in, you have 1,000 users and zero data on quality. When something breaks — you can't tell if it really broke.

Better: 30 examples from day one. Expand as you grow.

Second mistake: scoring only "correct / incorrect". AI quality is a spectrum: accuracy, style, length, tone. You need to measure several attributes separately.

sys-cost-management.title: How not to go broke on the AI API
sys-cost-management.what:
AI calls cost money. At launch — pennies. As you scale — can hit tens of thousands a month if you don't watch.

Cost Management is a set of simple practices: use the cheap model where you can, cache repeats, monitor spend daily. Not "optimization for its own sake" but "don't pay extra".
sys-cost-management.why:
AI spend grows silently. Today $50, in 3 months $5,000, another 3 — $30,000. Nobody notices because they're thinking "$0.001 per request — nothing".

If you monitor — you manage. If you don't — one day you get a bill and a shock.
sys-cost-management.when:
From day one in production (one of the core [[node:ai-operations|AI Operations]] practices). Not "when money becomes a problem" — by then the habit of overspending is set.

Signals you need cost management urgently:
- Don't know how much you spent last month
- Using the most expensive model "just in case"
- Not caching repeating requests
- Same AI calls in different parts of the product with different prompts
sys-cost-management.impact:
Without management: you overpay 3-5×. Part goes to "AI answers the same questions over and over", part to "using Opus where Haiku would do".

With management: spend is predictable, easy to plan. Often you can cut the bill 2-3× without losing quality.

Main point: you can run AI at scale without fearing the bill.
sys-cost-management.example:
SaaS chat support, 10,000 requests per day:

Before: all requests go through Sonnet, $0.015 per request → $4,500/month.

After:
1. AI first classifies the question type with cheap Haiku ($0.001)
2. Simple questions ("where's my invoice", "how to change password") → Haiku ($0.001)
3. Complex ("integration not working") → Sonnet ($0.015)
4. Very complex (~5%) → Opus with detailed analysis
5. FAQ answers cached → 30% of requests don't hit AI at all

Result: $1,200/month. Same or better quality (Opus where Sonnet used to struggle).
sys-cost-management.mistakes:
Main mistake: use the most powerful model "just in case". Opus costs 15× more than Haiku. On 80% of tasks the quality difference is invisible.

Better: cheap model by default, expensive only where really needed.

Second mistake: not caching repeating requests. If 30% of users ask the same FAQ — serve from cache, don't pay AI again.

sys-api-patterns.title: How AI talks to other systems
sys-api-patterns.what:
When AI needs to interact with your software (big topic — [[node:ai-integration-systems|AI Integration Systems]]) (CRM, email, database) — it goes through an API. There are 4 standard ways: reply immediately, kick off and report later, react to events, stream the answer piece by piece.

Picking the way = answering "how long does AI take" and "do we need the answer right now".
sys-api-patterns.why:
Wrong choice = AI is working, but the user sits staring at a spinner. Or the opposite: the user needs an instant answer, and you built a queue.

The right pattern = the user sees what they expect: "fast" when it's fast, "working on it" when it's slow.
sys-api-patterns.when:
**Reply immediately (sync)** — AI handles it in 1-3 seconds (short texts, classification, simple answers).

**Kick off and report (async)** — AI runs 30+ seconds (document analysis, big report generation). User starts → goes for coffee → gets a notification.

**By event (webhook)** — external trigger: email arrived / customer submitted a form / a task appeared.

**Piece by piece (streaming)** — long answer, user sees AI typing (like ChatGPT).
sys-api-patterns.impact:
Right pattern = UX doesn't annoy. The user either gets an answer instantly, or understands AI is working in the background, or sees progress.

Wrong = "clicked a button → waited 30 seconds staring at the screen". Half the users close the tab.

Main point: technology is tuned to user expectations, not the other way around.
sys-api-patterns.example:
AI assistant in a SaaS product:

1. **Sync**: "classify the task type" — 1 second, sync, button returns the answer immediately
2. **Async**: "full quarterly analysis" — 2 minutes, user kicks it off → keeps working → gets "report ready" notification
3. **Webhook**: a customer wrote in Intercom → external webhook triggers AI → AI drafts a reply in the agent's inbox
4. **Streaming**: "write a long email" — AI types piece by piece, user sees it being written, can interrupt if it's going off track

Each case — its own pattern. Don't try to do everything through one.
sys-api-patterns.mistakes:
Main mistake: do everything sync. User clicks a button → waits 40 seconds → nothing happens → closes the tab → AI finishes anyway → money spent, result is useless.

Better: if AI runs longer than 5 seconds — async with notification.

Second mistake: streaming where it's not needed. If the answer is short and arrives fast — streaming just complicates the code for no value.

sys-monitoring.title: Observability for AI systems
sys-monitoring.what:
Observability for AI is not "logs + uptime" — it's 5 specific metrics that show the health of a production system:

- **Latency** — p50/p95/p99 end-to-end (not just the API call, but with tool calls and retries)
- **Cost per call** — $/request broken down by feature and model (tightly tied to [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]])
- **Output token distribution** — histogram of response lengths; a sharp shift = the model has drifted or the prompt is broken
- **Tool-call success rate** — % of successful tool invocations vs schema errors / retries
- **Refusal rate** — % of responses where Claude refused (safety / ambiguity)

Tools: Datadog AI Observability, LangSmith, Honeycomb, Helicone — all ship AI-specific dashboards out of the box.
sys-monitoring.why:
Standard APM (CPU / RPS / 500s) only shows the API is alive. That doesn't mean the AI is doing its job. You can have 100% uptime and 40% garbage answers — regular monitoring won't catch it.

AI-specific metrics catch: silent quality drift (model answers, but worse), cost spikes (one user burns $500/day on long contexts), latency tail (p99 jumped from 3s to 12s — UX is dead for 1% of users).
sys-monitoring.when:
Day one in production. Latency and cost — mandatory immediately. Output distribution and refusal rate — from week two, once you have a baseline.

Signs monitoring is insufficient:
- You learn about issues from users, not from the dashboard
- You can't say how much a specific feature costs in $/day
- You can't answer "did it get worse after the last deploy?"
- One user can run up the bill without an alert
sys-monitoring.impact:
Concrete target values (as of writing 2026-05, typical for chat / agent workloads):
- p95 latency < 3s for interactive, < 30s for async agents
- p99 latency < 800ms on classification, < 8s on generation
- Tool-call success > 95% (otherwise prompt or schema is broken)
- Refusal rate < 2% (otherwise prompt needs review)
- Cost per call variance < 30% (otherwise runaway prompts)

With metrics: you catch regressions in hours, not days. Without: you find out when churn jumps 5%.
sys-monitoring.example:
SaaS feature "AI assistant in the email client", 50k requests/day.

Stack: Datadog AI Observability via middleware → traces with model, prompt_version, user_id, tokens_in/out, latency, tool_calls, refusal_flag.

Dashboard:
1. Top row: p50/p95/p99 latency + RPS + error rate
2. Cost panel: $/day split by feature (compose / summarize / classify), top-10 expensive users
3. Quality panel: output length histogram, tool success rate, refusal rate trend
4. Alerts: p99 > 8s (5min window), cost/hour > 2× rolling avg, refusal rate > 3%

Real incident: a prompt rewrite shipped → avg output length dropped from 180 to 40 tokens → alert in 12 minutes → rollback via [[node:sys-rollback-strategies|feature flag]] → fixed in an hour, not a week.
sys-monitoring.mistakes:
**1. Measuring latency only.** A fast response can be semantic garbage. Without refusal rate / output distribution, slow model degradation passes silently.

**2. Logging without aggregation.** 50k log lines a day is not observability — it's a dumpster. Metrics belong in Datadog / Prometheus; raw logs are for drill-down.

**3. Not splitting cost by feature.** "We spend $3000/mo on AI" — useless. "Compose costs $0.04/email, summarize $0.002" — actionable.

**4. Absolute alerts, not deviation alerts.** "p99 > 5s" fires 100×/day from batch jobs. "p99 grew 2× vs rolling 1h avg" — real regression.

**5. Ignoring tool-call metrics on agents.** If 30% of tool calls fail and retry — it's a cost spike, latency tail, and quality drop at once. The key metric for agents.

sys-logging-patterns.title: What to log for AI
sys-logging-patterns.what:
Logging for AI ≠ regular app logs. Minimum structured payload per call:

```json
{
  "request_id": "uuid",
  "timestamp": "...",
  "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5",
  "prompt_version": "v1.4.2",
  "prompt_hash": "sha256...",
  "input_tokens": 1240,
  "output_tokens": 380,
  "latency_ms": 2150,
  "tool_calls": [{"name": "...", "status": "ok"}],
  "user_id_hashed": "...",
  "feature": "email-compose"
}
```

Full prompt / completion live in a separate sampled store (10-20% of traffic), not in hot logs. That gives debug replay without $20k/mo in log storage.
sys-logging-patterns.why:
AI incidents are only diagnosable from prompt + completion + tool trace. Without them, "AI started hallucinating at customer X" is undiagnosable.

At the same time: prompts may contain user PII, completions may contain generated PII or secrets from tool calls. Wrong logging = GDPR incident or credential leak.

A logging pattern solves both: enough for debug, safe for compliance.
sys-logging-patterns.when:
From day one in production. Set sampling and retention from the start — retrofitting them in prod is expensive.

Signs logging is broken:
- "A user is complaining about a response from 3 days ago" — you can't reproduce
- You don't know which prompt version was active during the incident
- Logs take terabytes and cost more than the AI calls themselves
- You find API keys / emails / phones in plaintext in logs
sys-logging-patterns.impact:
**Must-log:** model, prompt_version, token counts, latency, tool_call statuses, feature/endpoint, hashed user_id.

**Sampled (10-20%):** full prompt, full completion, tool_call arguments + responses.

**Never log:** API keys, OAuth tokens, raw passwords, payment card numbers, SSN, plaintext PII (email/phone/address) — redact in the SDK layer via regex or token-level redaction.

**Retention (typical):** hot logs 7d (fast debug), warm 30d (post-mortem), cold 90d (compliance / audit). Full prompts — sampled, retention 14-30d max. Longer = GDPR risk and cost spike.
sys-logging-patterns.example:
B2B email AI, 100k requests/day.

1. Middleware wraps the Anthropic SDK → structured log to Datadog (metadata only, no prompt/completion bodies) → 100% of requests.
2. 15% sampled → separate S3 bucket with full payload, encrypted at rest, lifecycle policy: hot 7d → cold 30d → delete.
3. PII redactor (see [[node:pl-privacy|privacy]]) in middleware: regex for email/phone + Anthropic Claude Haiku detector for names — replaces with `[REDACTED:type]` BEFORE logging.
4. Prompt version = git SHA from CI → connects logs with [[node:sys-versioning|prompt version]] in code.
5. Incident replay: feed request_id → middleware pulls sampled payload + metadata + model version → reproduce locally.

Result: incidents resolvable in minutes, log cost under $200/mo, GDPR audit passes.
sys-logging-patterns.mistakes:
**1. Logging everything to hot storage.** 100k requests × 5k tokens × 4 bytes = ~2GB/day in prompts alone. A year = $30k+ in Datadog. Sample full payloads, aggregate metadata.

**2. PII in plaintext.** The most common incident. Email AI logs full email body → grabs the customer's email → GDPR violation. Redact BEFORE writing, not after.

**3. Logging API secrets.** Tool calls often carry credentials in arguments (`{"db_password": "..."}`). Whitelist fields you log from tool_args, don't blacklist.

**4. Not logging prompt_version.** In 3 months you can't tie a "bad answer" to a specific prompt version. Pin to git SHA — required (see [[node:sys-versioning|sys-versioning]]).

**5. Infinite retention.** "We keep it for a year just in case." GDPR requires deletion, storage grows linearly, value drops exponentially. 7/30/90 is the standard.

sys-versioning.title: Prompt and model versioning
sys-versioning.what:
Prompts are code. That means they need semver, lock files, review, and diff history. Two layers:

**Layer 1 — prompt version:** prompts live in `prompts/*.md` or `prompts.yaml` in git, semver (`v1.4.2`), PR review, every AI request injects `prompt_version` for tracing.

**Layer 2 — model version:** **pinning** (`claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`) vs **auto-update** (`claude-sonnet-4-5`). Pinning = determinism, manual upgrade. Auto-update = automatic improvements, risk of unannounced regression.

Lock file `models.lock.json` with concrete snapshot IDs for every model in the system — analogous to `package-lock.json`.
sys-versioning.why:
Without versioning, "AI worked yesterday, not today" is undebuggable. Did the prompt change? Did the model auto-update? Did Anthropic roll out a new model? — no answers without versions.

With versioning, every response is tied to (prompt_vN, model_snapshot) → the diff between "working" and "broken" is in git.
sys-versioning.when:
From the moment a prompt ships to real users. Pre-production you can live with inline prompts; in prod without versions you're flying blind.

Signs versioning is urgent:
- The prompt changes, nobody remembers when or why
- You use a model alias (no snapshot) and don't know when Anthropic will update it
- No eval process before bumping the model — you upgrade and pray
- Rolling back a prompt = git revert + redeploy the whole service (no hot-swap)
sys-versioning.impact:
**Pinning vs auto-update (as of writing 2026-05):**

- **Pin to snapshot** (`claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`) — production-grade. Anthropic maintains old snapshots ~12 months, deprecation announced ahead of time. Your code is stable, upgrade is your call.
- **Alias** (`claude-sonnet-4-5`) — resolves to the latest snapshot. Convenient for dev / playground. In production = risk of "Anthropic ships in the morning, your regression hits in the evening".

**Eval gate on model bump:** before swapping a snapshot, run the [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|eval suite]] (50-200 cases). Pass rate must not drop by >2%. If it does — don't ship.

**Prompt semver:** patch = wording / typo, minor = new rules without breaking, major = output schema change → forced re-eval of all downstream consumers.
sys-versioning.example:
B2B SaaS, 8 prompts in production.

```yaml
# prompts/email-compose.yaml
id: email-compose
version: 2.3.1
model: claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929  # PINNED
template: |
  You are an email assistant...
```

```json
// models.lock.json
{
  "claude-sonnet-4-5": "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
  "claude-haiku-4-5": "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"
}
```

Flow:
1. PR changes email-compose.yaml → bump `version: 2.4.0` → review required from 2 people
2. CI runs eval suite on new version vs production → diff report in PR
3. If pass rate ≥ baseline-2% → merge → deploy
4. Every AI call logs `prompt_version: 2.4.0` (see [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging]])
5. Anthropic announces sonnet-4-6 → PR opened to bump the lock file → eval suite on new model → if green, merge 1-2 weeks after release, not day-of

Rollback on regression: git revert PR → CI redeploy in 5 minutes, or [[node:sys-rollback-strategies|feature flag]] to the old version instantly.
sys-versioning.mistakes:
**1. Using a model alias in production.** `claude-sonnet-4-5` without a snapshot = ticking bomb. Anthropic publishes a deprecation policy — pin snapshots, upgrade consciously.

**2. Prompts in code instead of git-versioned files.** "We changed the prompt in `app.py` line 234" — no diff history, no review, no rollback. Prompts go in dedicated files, like config.

**3. Bumping the model without evals.** "A new model is out, we upgraded" → 20% of answers got worse → you find out via NPS a week later. **Always** an eval gate before a production switch.

**4. Semver without rules.** `v1`, `v1.1`, `v2` without understanding patch/minor/major. The team doesn't know whether a bump is safe to merge. Document the rules in `prompts/README.md`.

**5. Not versioning tool definitions.** Tool schema is part of the prompt. Change the schema → the model behaves differently. Lock both schema and version.

*deprecate-watch: as of 2026-05 Anthropic's policy is ~12 months of snapshot support after deprecation. Check [docs.anthropic.com](https://docs.anthropic.com) — the window can change.*

sys-rollback-strategies.title: Rollback on regression
sys-rollback-strategies.what:
When a new prompt or model version starts answering worse, you need fast rollback **without a full redeploy**. Three layers:

1. **Feature flags** (LaunchDarkly / Unleash / homegrown) — switch prompt_version or model snapshot for a % of traffic. Rollback = flip toggle, seconds.
2. **Canary deployment** — new version rolls 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% with auto-rollback on metrics drift.
3. **Kill switch** — a global rubber band: turn the AI feature off entirely, fall back to rule-based / human queue / cached responses. For catastrophic failures (model hallucinating en masse, refusal rate spiked).

All built on [[node:sys-versioning|versioning]] (what to roll back) and [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]] (when to roll back).
sys-rollback-strategies.why:
Time from detection to rollback = MTTR. Without infrastructure: detect → debug → fix → PR → CI → deploy = hours or days. With feature flags: detect → flip → seconds.

In AI systems regressions are quieter than in regular code (no stack trace), but more expensive (bad answers to customers = trust damage). MTTR must be in minutes, not hours.
sys-rollback-strategies.when:
Once an AI feature becomes revenue-critical or customer-facing. Internal tooling can live with git-revert rollbacks. Customer-facing — must have a flag or canary.

Signs:
- Last incident: regression lived 6+ hours before fix
- The team is afraid to ship prompt changes (= ship rarely, in big batches = higher risk)
- No way to compare v1 vs v2 on live traffic (only in evals)
- The only path on issues is git revert + full redeploy
sys-rollback-strategies.impact:
**Concrete targets for production AI (2026-05 baseline):**
- MTTR from alert to rollback < 5 minutes
- Canary stages: 1% (24h) → 10% (24h) → 50% (24h) → 100%
- Auto-rollback triggers: refusal rate +50% vs baseline, p99 latency 2× baseline, eval score drop >5%, cost/request +30%
- Kill switch coverage: every AI feature must have a fallback path (even if it's "feature unavailable, try later")

Tools: LaunchDarkly / Unleash / Statsig for flags, Argo Rollouts / Flagger for canary on Kubernetes, custom middleware for AI-specific metrics in triggers.
sys-rollback-strategies.example:
AI email-compose in SaaS, deploy v2.4 (new prompt).

1. PR merged → CI built → feature flag `email_compose_v2_4` created in LaunchDarkly, default = 0%.
2. Canary stage 1: flag = 1% of users (random hash) → watch dashboard 24h → refusal rate, latency, output length, NPS proxy (% click "regenerate").
3. Stage 2: 10% → 24h watch. Metrics in band → continue.
4. At stage 3 (50%): refusal rate jumped 1.2% → 3.8% (alert via [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]).
5. Auto-rollback rule fires: flag → 0% in 30 seconds. All users back on v2.3.1.
6. Post-mortem: new prompt triggers a safety filter on an edge case. Fix it, ship v2.4.1, restart canary.

**Kill switch test:** quarterly game day. Turn the AI feature off entirely, verify the fallback (template-based draft) works and UX doesn't fall into null.
sys-rollback-strategies.mistakes:
**1. Feature flag without auto-rollback.** Human watches the dashboard → spots regression → flips by hand. 15-30 minutes pass between detection and flip. Triggers must be automated.

**2. Canary without statistical significance.** 1% traffic × 1 hour = 50 requests. Any difference is noise. Minimum 24h per stage, or N >= 1000 requests per comparison.

**3. Kill switch without a fallback path.** "Turned AI off → blank screen for the user." Kill switch must include **graceful degradation**: template response, human queue, cached answer, "feature unavailable".

**4. Rolling back the prompt only, not the model.** If a model bump caused the regression — the flag should toggle both `prompt_version` and `model_snapshot`. They're often coupled.

**5. Testing rollback only in prod.** Quarterly game day: simulate a regression → verify rollback completes in < 5 minutes. Otherwise you discover the broken kill switch the moment you need it.

sys-rate-limiting.title: Rate limiting and backoff
sys-rate-limiting.what:
Two related but distinct layers:

**Internal rate limiting** — you cap your own traffic to Anthropic so you don't hit [[node:pl-rate|tier limits]] and trigger a 429 cascade.
- Token bucket / leaky bucket algorithms
- Per-user quotas (one user can't burn the whole tier)
- Priority queues (interactive > batch)

**Backoff on errors** — what to do when the API returns 429 / 529 / 5xx.
- Exponential backoff: delay = `base × 2^attempt`, base = 1-2s
- Jitter ±20% (prevents thundering herd on simultaneous retries)
- Respect `retry-after` header — Anthropic suggests the optimal delay
- Max retries 3-5; beyond that — circuit breaker

**Circuit breaker** — after N consecutive failures (5-10) fail fast (open state) → probe after timeout (half-open) → recovery (closed). Protects from cascades during long outages.
sys-rate-limiting.why:
Without rate limiting: one runaway script or viral spike → 429 across the whole tier → even interactive users get errors → trust damage.

Without backoff: retries on 429 burn your own quota → more 429s → cascade failure.

Without a circuit breaker: during an Anthropic outage retry storms generate $1000+ in failed calls and clog the system with wait blocks.
sys-rate-limiting.when:
Backoff + retry — from the first production call. Internal rate limiting — when you have ≥3 traffic sources to the API (interactive, batch, async jobs) or you're on Tier 2+. Circuit breaker — when the service is customer-facing and SLA matters.

Signs of gaps:
- One batch job tanks interactive users
- On 429 you see a retry spike in logs (= dumb retry without backoff)
- Anthropic outage = your service hangs on 30+ second timeouts instead of fail-fast
- No per-user quotas — one user can blow everyone's budget
sys-rate-limiting.impact:
**Concrete numbers (2026-05 baseline):**
- Exponential backoff: `delay = min(2^attempt × 1000ms, 60s)` + jitter ±20%
- Max retries: 3 for interactive (better to fail fast), 5-7 for batch (acceptable to wait)
- Internal limit: 80% of the Anthropic tier limit (see [[node:pl-rate|pl-rate]]) — buffer for spikes
- Circuit breaker thresholds: open after 5 fails / 30s, half-open after 30s timeout, closed after 3 consecutive successes
- Per-user quota: typically 100 req/min for interactive, 1000/day for chat

Use Anthropic's **Message Batches API** for non-realtime workloads — separate rate-limit pool, 50% discount, ideal for evals / classification.
sys-rate-limiting.mistakes:
**1. Retry without exponential backoff.** Linear retry (1s, 1s, 1s) on 429 = you burn your own quota. Always exponential + jitter.

**2. Ignoring the `retry-after` header.** Anthropic returns an optimal delay in the header. Dumb backoff ignores it and retries too early → another 429. Parse the header, use it as a minimum.

**3. Infinite retry.** "We'll try until it works." On a transient outage = $$$ in failed calls + clogged worker threads. Max 3-7 attempts, then fail fast → fallback.

**4. One rate limit for everything.** Mixing interactive and batch in one pool → batch eats the quota → interactive drops. Minimum 2 pools: interactive priority high, batch low. Use the Message Batches API for offline loads.

**5. No per-user quotas.** One user (or a compromised API key) can burn the whole tier in an hour. Per user_id quota is mandatory for multi-tenant.

*deprecate-watch: specific RPM/TPM tier limits at Anthropic shift (see [[node:pl-rate|pl-rate]]); the bucket+backoff+breaker pattern is stable.*

sys-semantic-cache.title: Semantic cache
sys-semantic-cache.what:
Beyond [[node:cap-caching|prompt caching]] (which caches the **prefix** of the same text) — **semantic cache** caches the **meaning** of a query.

Mechanics: on an incoming request compute an embedding ([[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]]) → search [[node:af-vector-db|vector DB]] for similar prior queries → if cosine similarity > threshold (typically 0.92-0.97) and context is compatible → return the cached completion, skip the AI call.

Essentially: "has anyone asked this in meaning over the last 30 days? If yes — return their answer."

Tools: GPTCache, Helicone semantic cache, custom on pgvector + Redis.
sys-semantic-cache.why:
Prompt cache saves on the repeating **prefix** (system prompt, knowledge base). Semantic cache saves on repeating **questions** — even when phrased differently.

In FAQ-shaped loads 30-40% of queries are rephrasings of the same questions. Prompt cache doesn't catch them (the user query differs). Semantic cache does — returning an answer in 50ms instead of 2s + $0.

The two are orthogonal and combine: prompt cache on prefix + semantic cache on the full query.
sys-semantic-cache.when:
**Works well:**
- FAQ / support — same questions, different wording
- Classification — fixed category set, repeating inputs
- Docs search — same queries across users
- Translation of popular phrases

**Doesn't work:**
- Creative generation (every response must be fresh)
- Real-time data ("what's in the news today") — cached answer goes stale
- Personalized completions (response depends on user_context) — can't share across users
- Chat with history (the history is part of the query, semantic match impossible)

**Signs semantic cache will pay off:**
- Prompt cache miss rate is already low but cost stays high
- Logs show "the same question phrased differently from different users"
- Read-heavy workload (classification, FAQ, search)
sys-semantic-cache.impact:
**Typical performance (2026-05 baselines):**
- Cache hit rate: 30-40% on FAQ loads, 50-60% on classification with fixed categories, < 5% on creative
- Latency on hit: 30-80ms (embedding + vector search + return) vs 1-5s on AI call
- Cost savings: 30-50% of total spend on read-heavy workloads (after prompt caching)
- Similarity threshold: 0.95 — balance of recall / precision; > 0.97 — strict (few false hits, lower hit rate); < 0.92 — risky (you get a similar-but-not-the-same answer)

**Cache invalidation strategies:**
- TTL-based: 1h for volatile, 24h for FAQ, 7d for stable knowledge
- Event-driven: when the knowledge base changes — purge all cached completions referencing that section
- Version-keyed: cache key includes prompt_version + knowledge_base_version → bump → automatic invalidation
sys-semantic-cache.example:
Customer support AI, 20k requests/day, typical question "how do I cancel my subscription".

Stack: pgvector + Redis for embedding cache + custom middleware.

```python
def answer(question, user_context):
    if not user_context.is_personalized():
        emb = embed(question)
        # cosine sim search in pgvector
        hit = vector_db.search(emb, threshold=0.95, k=1)
        if hit and hit.is_fresh(ttl_hours=24):
            metrics.inc("semantic_cache_hit")
            return hit.cached_completion
    
    # Cache miss → real AI call
    completion = claude.complete(question, context=user_context)
    if not user_context.is_personalized():
        vector_db.store(emb, completion, ttl_hours=24)
    return completion
```

Metrics after 2 weeks:
- Hit rate: 34% on support queue
- Avg latency: 1800ms → 1200ms (combined)
- AI spend: $2400/mo → $1580/mo (-34%)
- p95 latency on hit: 65ms (vector lookup + Redis fetch)

Combined with [[node:cap-caching|prompt caching]] on the remaining 66%: total cost down 60%+ vs naive baseline.
sys-semantic-cache.mistakes:
**1. Threshold too low.** Similarity 0.85 = semantically close, not identical. "How do I cancel my subscription?" matches "How do I change my subscription?" → customer gets a cancellation answer instead of upgrade → trust damage. Start at 0.95, validate on real queries.

**2. Caching personalized completions.** User A asks "when is my next payment" → cache → User B with the same question gets User A's payment date. GDPR cascade + reputation hit. Personalized = NO cache.

**3. No invalidation strategy.** Knowledge base updated → cached answers go stale → customers get stale info for weeks. Version the cache key or do event-driven purge.

**4. Semantic cache on creative content.** "Write a welcome email" — every user wants their own. Cache hit = everyone gets the same email = obviously robotic.

**5. Ignoring embedding cost itself.** Embedding on every request costs money and latency (cheaper than LLM, but not free). If hit rate < 10% — net cost is negative. Measure break-even hit rate for your workload.

sys-branching-logic.title: Branching logic in workflows
sys-branching-logic.what:
Conditional branching in AI workflows: after step A, the model — not the user, not hardcoded if/else — decides whether to go to B or C.

Three common implementations:

- **Prompt-driven routing** — a separate classification call (often Haiku) returns a category; code then routes on it. Cheap, easy to debug.
- **Structured outputs / tool use** — the main model emits `{decision: "refund" | "escalate" | "answer"}` via JSON schema or tool definition in one call. Faster, costs more tokens.
- **Embedding similarity routing** — the input is embedded and compared to category prototypes. No LLM call, but needs curated examples.

The key is an explicit **decision schema** (closed list of options), not free text.
sys-branching-logic.why:
Without branching, a workflow becomes either one giant "do everything" prompt — unpredictable quality, expensive — or rigid regex if/else that breaks on any new case.

With branching, each branch is its own optimized prompt; the router picks the branch; debugging is local to one branch, not the monolith.
sys-branching-logic.when:
When a workflow has 3+ fundamentally different scenarios on the same input. Examples:

- Customer support: refund / how-to / bug-report with different prompts and tools
- Email triage: spam / sales / urgent with different actions
- Code review: security / style / logic with different specialists

Signals you need branching:
- One prompt "does 5 different things badly"
- Output structure varies by input type
- You want different models per scenario for cost reasons
sys-branching-logic.impact:
**Decision schema structure (production baseline, 2026-05):**

- Closed enum of branches (3-7, not 20)
- A `confidence: 0..1` field from the router for [[node:sys-confidence-thresholds|confidence thresholds]]
- A `reason: string` field for debugging in [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logs]]
- A default `unknown` branch — escalates to human or falls back to a generic prompt

**Cost optimization:** router on Haiku ($0.25/1M in), specialist branches on Sonnet. Typically 5-10x cheaper than "one big Sonnet call does everything."

**Latency:** sequential branching adds one LLM hop (200-500ms on Haiku). If latency-critical, use a structured output in the main call (one hop, more expensive).
sys-branching-logic.example:
SaaS helpdesk, 12k tickets/day.

```python
# Step 1: router (Haiku)
router_prompt = """Categorize this support ticket.
Return JSON: {category: "refund"|"how-to"|"bug"|"feature-request"|"other",
             confidence: 0..1, reason: string}"""
routing = claude_haiku.messages.create(prompt=router_prompt + ticket)

# Step 2: branch
if routing.confidence < 0.7:
    return escalate_to_human(ticket, reason=routing.reason)

branch = {
    "refund": refund_specialist_prompt,    # Sonnet + tools(billing_api)
    "how-to": kb_search_prompt,            # Sonnet + tools(search_kb)
    "bug": bug_triage_prompt,              # Sonnet + tools(linear_create)
    "feature-request": feedback_log_prompt,
    "other": general_assistant_prompt,
}[routing.category]

response = claude_sonnet.messages.create(
    prompt=branch + ticket,
    metadata={"prompt_version": "router-1.2.0", "branch": routing.category}
)
```

Dashboard ([[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]): branch distribution, router accuracy (via human-review sampling), confidence distribution. If 30% lands in `other`, you need a new branch.
sys-branching-logic.mistakes:
**1. Open text output instead of an enum.** "Describe the category in one word" — the model writes "Refund Request" instead of "refund" 5% of the time, routing breaks. Always closed enum via JSON schema or tool use.

**2. No default branch.** Router returns something unexpected, code crashes. Always default to fallback or escalation.

**3. Ignoring confidence.** A router with confidence=0.3 confidently routes to `refund`, the specialist runs a refund flow on a bug complaint. Minimum: confidence < 0.7 triggers [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation]].

**4. Too many branches.** 15 categories confuse the router below 70% accuracy. Cap at 5-7 branches; otherwise build a hierarchy (router into sub-router).

**5. Branching without logging the decision.** A ticket ends up in the wrong place, no way to inspect what the router decided. Always log `(input_hash, category, confidence, reason)`.

sys-loop-patterns.title: Loop patterns: refine until quality
sys-loop-patterns.what:
Refinement loops — a workflow repeats a step (or a chain of steps) until a quality criterion is met or an iteration budget is exhausted.

Three canonical patterns:

- **Critique-revise loop** — generator produces output, critic finds issues, generator rewrites with feedback, repeat. Quality grows, tokens grow linearly.
- **Tool-use loop** (ReAct-style) — the model thinks, calls a tool, sees the result, thinks again, calls the next tool, then finishes. Natural for agents.
- **Convergence loop** — two variants are generated and compared; if they agree (via LLM judge or embedding similarity > threshold), finish.

Every loop needs **max-iterations guard** (3-10) and **convergence detection**, otherwise costs run away.
sys-loop-patterns.why:
Single-pass prompts are bounded — the model cannot "rewrite considering the issue" unless explicitly asked. A loop gives self-correction without human intervention.

Without loops, quality is capped by what the model produces in one shot. Without guards, one buggy case burns $50 on a single request.
sys-loop-patterns.when:
When input varies and quality cannot be fixed in one prompt:

- Code generation (working code is the target, not "an attempt")
- Long-form writing with criteria (research reports, structured docs)
- Multi-step agents (browsing, research, multi-step calculations)
- Analysis with clarifying questions

Signals you need a loop:
- Output is often "almost right" — one revision fixes it
- A measurable quality criterion exists (compile, test pass, schema valid, judge score)
- Cost of error > cost of 2-3x LLM calls
sys-loop-patterns.impact:
**Production parameters (2026-05):**

- Max iterations: 3 for interactive (UX), 5-10 for async (research, code-gen)
- Convergence threshold: LLM judge score >= 8/10, embedding cosine > 0.92
- Cost guard: hard cap $X per request (3-5x average) — fail fast
- Time guard: total wall-clock < 30s interactive, < 5min async

Quality effect: critique-revise loops typically add +15-25% pass rate on code-gen vs single-shot. Cost: 2.5-3x tokens.

Combine with [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|eval suite]] — each iteration is logged, and the max-iterations setting is calibrated on real data.
sys-loop-patterns.example:
AI code-review bot for PRs in a B2B SaaS.

```python
MAX_ITER = 5
QUALITY_THRESHOLD = 8  # out of 10
COST_LIMIT_USD = 0.50

def review_pr(diff):
    cost = 0
    review = generate_review(diff)  # initial pass, Sonnet
    cost += track_cost(review)

    for iteration in range(MAX_ITER):
        critique = critic_call(diff, review)  # Haiku, cheap
        cost += track_cost(critique)

        if critique.score >= QUALITY_THRESHOLD:
            return review, {"iterations": iteration, "cost": cost}

        if cost > COST_LIMIT_USD:
            log_overflow(diff, cost)
            return review, {"iterations": iteration, "cost": cost, "overflow": True}

        review = generate_review(diff, prior_review=review,
                                  feedback=critique.issues)  # Sonnet
        cost += track_cost(review)

    log_max_iter_hit(diff)
    return review, {"iterations": MAX_ITER, "cost": cost}
```

Metrics ([[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]): iterations histogram (norm: 90% finish in <=2 iterations), max-iter-hit rate (alert > 5%), cost-overflow rate (alert > 1%), critic score distribution.
sys-loop-patterns.mistakes:
**1. No max-iterations.** "Iterate until perfect" — one edge case burns $50 and ties up a worker for 10 minutes. Hard limit, always.

**2. Critic is the same model as the generator.** Sonnet generating, Sonnet critiquing — the model cannot see its own errors (motivated reasoning). Use a different model or a radically different prompt framing.

**3. No cost guard.** Iterations cap is in place, but one prompt with a long context times 5 iterations = $5 per request. Add a cost cap.

**4. Loop without logging intermediate steps.** Final output is captured, iterations are lost — you cannot tell where the model "got lost." Log each iteration (see [[node:sys-logging-patterns|logging]]).

**5. Convergence via text equality.** "Two outputs are identical, finish" works 5% of the time. Use semantic similarity (embeddings) or an LLM judge.

sys-prompt-chaining.title: Prompt chaining: composition
sys-prompt-chaining.what:
A chain of prompts — output of one call becomes input to the next: `A -> B -> C`. Unlike [[node:sys-linear-chain|sys-linear-chain]] (the general concept of sequential workflows), prompt chaining focuses on the **mechanics of passing data** between steps.

Three mandatory aspects:

- **Schema at every boundary** — output of A is validated as `{field1, field2, ...}` via JSON schema or Pydantic before hitting B. Without it, the model changes format and the chain breaks silently.
- **Error propagation** — step B knows what to do if A returned an error, low quality, or a partial result: skip, retry, fall back, ask human.
- **Idempotency** — re-running the chain with the same inputs should yield the same output (or explicit nondeterminism). Otherwise debugging is impossible.
sys-prompt-chaining.why:
Without explicit decomposition, one monster prompt — "extract entities, classify them, write a summary, suggest actions" — works 70% of the time and fails 30% in ways no one can localize.

A chain lets you debug each step in isolation, swap the model per step (Haiku for extraction, Sonnet for writing), cache intermediate results, and insert human review between steps.
sys-prompt-chaining.when:
Workflows with 2+ logically distinct tasks on the same data:

- Research -> summarize -> format
- Extract entities -> classify -> write report
- Parse contract -> identify clauses -> flag risks
- Transcribe -> analyze sentiment -> generate reply

When not to use it: single-step tasks (classification, simple generation). A 2-step chain on a simple task adds latency with no gain.
sys-prompt-chaining.impact:
**Cost of cascading errors:** if each step is 95% accurate, a 4-step chain is 81% end-to-end. Quality gates ([[node:sys-quality-gates|quality gates]]) at every boundary are mandatory.

**Latency:** sequential — sums up (4 steps × 800ms = 3.2s). Parallelize where possible (see [[node:sys-parallel-fan-out|parallel fan-out]]).

**Cost optimization (2026-05):**
- Extraction / classification -> Haiku ($0.25/1M in)
- Writing / reasoning -> Sonnet ($3/1M in)
- Final critique -> Haiku
Typically 3-5x cheaper than "Sonnet at every step."

**Caching:** intermediate results with deterministic prompts go to a cache (Redis, 1-24h TTL) — re-running the final step costs nothing.
sys-prompt-chaining.mistakes:
**1. Passing raw text between steps.** Step A returns prose, step B parses it with regex — 10% of the time it breaks. Always JSON schema at the boundary.

**2. Not validating step N output before step N+1.** The model returns `null` instead of an array once in 100 calls, step N+1 crashes 30 seconds later with a cryptic error. Validate at the boundary and fail fast.

**3. Identical prompts with the same model at every step.** Sonnet on an extraction task costs ~12x more than needed. Pick the model per step.

**4. No error-propagation strategy.** Step A produces a weak result, B takes it as-is, C draws conclusions from garbage. At each step, an explicit branch: skip, retry, fall back, escalate.

**5. Chain without a `trace_id`.** Logs show separate calls and you cannot reassemble the request. Each step gets and forwards a `trace_id` — debug time drops 10x.

sys-vector-stores.title: Vector stores: choosing one
sys-vector-stores.what:
A vector store is a database for embeddings with fast ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) search. It powers RAG ([[node:sys-rag-architecture|sys-rag-architecture]]), semantic search, and [[node:sys-semantic-cache|semantic cache]].

Top choices (production, 2026-05):

- **pgvector** (Postgres extension) — embedded in your DB, transactions, joins, role-based access. Scales comfortably to ~10M vectors. Free.
- **Pinecone** — managed SaaS, serverless tier, simple API, good for PoC and mid-scale prod. Paid ($70+/mo base).
- **Qdrant** — open-source / cloud, rich filtering (metadata + vector), strong performance, self-host option.
- **Weaviate** — open-source, modular embedders, GraphQL API, hybrid search built in.
- **Chroma** — simple, embed-friendly, good for PoC and small prod. Not for hundreds of millions of vectors.
sys-vector-stores.why:
Vector store choice drives three critical things: operational complexity (managed vs self-host), latency at scale, and cost. A wrong call at the start means weeks of migration work later.

Most teams start with overkill (Pinecone when pgvector is plenty) or underkill (Chroma when they need managed). Both hurt to fix.
sys-vector-stores.when:
You need a vector store once you have >10k documents or do RAG in production.

Decision factors:

- **Already on Postgres, < 5M vectors, < 100 QPS** -> **pgvector** (no new infra)
- **No ops team, want managed, budget OK** -> **Pinecone** or **Qdrant Cloud**
- **Complex filters (metadata + vector), self-host** -> **Qdrant**
- **Hybrid search out of the box** -> **Weaviate** (or pgvector + BM25 by hand)
- **PoC on a laptop** -> **Chroma**
sys-vector-stores.impact:
**Latency budget (single query, top-10, 1M vectors, 2026-05):**
- pgvector with HNSW: 20-80ms p95
- Pinecone serverless: 50-150ms p95 (network round-trip)
- Qdrant self-host: 10-40ms p95
- Weaviate: 30-100ms p95

**Cost (1M vectors of 1536-dim, 100 QPS):**
- pgvector: cost of your Postgres + ~$0 extra
- Pinecone: ~$70-300/mo serverless
- Qdrant Cloud: ~$100-400/mo
- Self-host Qdrant: VM cost (1-2 vCPU, 4-8GB RAM) ~$30-80/mo

**Operational complexity:**
- Managed (Pinecone, Qdrant Cloud) = 0 ops
- Self-host = backups, upgrades, monitoring (plan 4-8h/mo)

Combine with [[node:sys-chunking-strategies|chunking]] and [[node:sys-hybrid-search|hybrid search]] — a store without proper data prep is useless.
sys-vector-stores.example:
B2B SaaS, knowledge base of 200k support docs, 50 QPS, ops team of 2, already on Postgres RDS.

Choice: **pgvector**.

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION vector;
CREATE TABLE doc_chunks (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  doc_id UUID REFERENCES docs(id),
  chunk_text TEXT,
  embedding vector(1536),
  metadata JSONB,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX ON doc_chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);
CREATE INDEX ON doc_chunks USING GIN (metadata);
```

Query: `SELECT chunk_text FROM doc_chunks WHERE metadata->>'product' = 'enterprise' ORDER BY embedding <=> $query_embedding LIMIT 10;`

Latency: 30-50ms p95 on 200k chunks. Backups run with Postgres. Access uses the same role-based permissions.

A year later: 5M chunks, p95 latency 120ms — migrate to dedicated Qdrant with metadata as payload. The migration is one script over 2 days, not weeks.
sys-vector-stores.mistakes:
**1. Pinecone "because it is popular" at 50k vectors with Postgres available.** You pay $70/mo for a feature pgvector has for free and faster (no network hop).

**2. Chroma in production.** Chroma is for PoCs. At 1M+ vectors or >50 QPS it becomes operational pain (no HA, no managed backup, no mature replication).

**3. Ignoring metadata filtering.** Vector-only search returns the top 10 "similar texts" from 5 different products and the user sees noise. Always filter by `tenant_id`, `product`, `lang`, `date_range` before the vector search.

**4. One index across all tenants.** Multi-tenant without namespace/partition: one tenant sees another's data — security incident. Use namespaces (Pinecone) / partitions (Qdrant) / `WHERE tenant_id = ?` (pgvector).

**5. Re-embed without re-index.** You change the embedding model and old vectors are incompatible with new ones — results degrade. Full re-indexing is required; ideally parallel indexes with A/B routing.

*deprecate-watch: the vector-DB landscape moves fast — latency/cost numbers are a 2026-05 baseline.*

sys-chunking-strategies.title: Chunking strategies
sys-chunking-strategies.what:
Splitting documents into chunks before embedding is the foundational step of a RAG pipeline. Retrieval quality depends on chunking more than on the vector store or embedding model choice.

Four strategies:

- **Fixed-size** — N tokens (usually 256-512) with 10-20% overlap. Simple, fast, loses context at boundaries.
- **Recursive splitter** (LangChain RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter) — splits by paragraph, sentence, word, recursively until each piece fits. Good for prose.
- **Semantic chunking** — adjacent sentences are compared by embedding similarity; a chunk boundary lands where similarity drops (topic shift). Costly to ingest, better retrieval.
- **Document-aware** — respects structure (markdown headings, HTML tags, code blocks). A chunk is a logical section, not an arbitrary window.

Every chunk carries **metadata**: source_id, position, parent_section, author, date.
sys-chunking-strategies.why:
Bad chunking breaks everything downstream. Chunks too large — embeddings get diluted ("average meaning" vectors), top-N includes garbage context. Chunks too small — context is lost and the model has no idea what the snippet is about.

When diagnosing "why is RAG answering poorly," chunking is the culprit 60-70% of the time, not the model.
sys-chunking-strategies.when:
From day one of any RAG system. Strategy depends on content type:

- **Prose / articles / docs** -> recursive splitter (fast, sufficient)
- **Mixed format (code + text)** -> document-aware with per-block-type splitting
- **Long structured documents** (contracts, research papers) -> semantic chunking
- **Tabular / structured data** -> row-based, not text-based

Signals chunking is broken:
- Retrieved chunks answer "almost your question," not your actual one
- The model cites a piece of text mid-sentence
- One document occupies 8 of the top-10 (over-chunking)
sys-chunking-strategies.impact:
**Production baseline (2026-05):**

- **Chunk size**: 256-512 tokens for prose, 128-256 for FAQ-style content, 512-1024 for technical docs
- **Overlap**: 10-20% (50-100 tokens on a 512 chunk) — critical so a boundary-straddling fact is not lost
- **Metadata always**: `{source_id, doc_title, section, page, position, lang, updated_at}` — for filtering and citations
- **Embedding model**: should match chunk size (`text-embedding-3-small` handles up to 8k tokens, but 256-512 is the sweet spot)

**Ingestion cost (1M documents, avg 5k tokens, chunk=512):**
- Fixed/recursive: ~10M chunks × $0.02/1M = $200 one-shot
- Semantic: 2-5x more expensive (extra embedding calls for boundary detection)

Combine with [[node:sys-hybrid-search|hybrid search]] — chunking decides what is retrievable at all.
sys-chunking-strategies.example:
B2B knowledge base: a mix of markdown docs, Slack threads, and PDF contracts.

```python
from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

# Strategy 1: Markdown docs
md_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    separators=["\n## ", "\n### ", "\n\n", "\n", " "],
    chunk_size=512, chunk_overlap=80,
    length_function=token_count  # tiktoken-based
)

# Strategy 2: Slack threads (preserve message boundaries)
slack_chunks = [{"text": msg.text, "metadata": {...}} for msg in thread]
# Do not split messages

# Strategy 3: PDF contracts (semantic)
from langchain_experimental.text_splitter import SemanticChunker
sem_splitter = SemanticChunker(embeddings, breakpoint_threshold_type="percentile")
contract_chunks = sem_splitter.create_documents([contract_text])

# Universal metadata
for chunk in all_chunks:
    chunk.metadata.update({
        "source_id": doc_id, "source_type": type, "section": heading,
        "lang": detect_lang(chunk.text), "updated_at": doc.updated_at,
        "tenant_id": tenant
    })
```

If retrieval recall on the eval set is <70%, A/B chunk_size (256 vs 512 vs 1024) and overlap (10% vs 20%) — that usually gains +10-15% without swapping the model.
sys-chunking-strategies.mistakes:
**1. One chunk_size for everything.** A PDF contract and an FAQ page need different treatment. Pick by `source_type`.

**2. No overlap.** A fact at a chunk boundary is lost — half in one vector, half in another, neither is relevant. Use at least 10% overlap.

**3. Splitting structured blocks.** A table split across 3 chunks is meaningless; a split code block breaks syntax. Detect blocks and keep them intact.

**4. Chunks without metadata.** Retrieved chunk = bare text with no source — no citations, no filtering by tenant/language/date. Metadata is mandatory from day one.

**5. Not re-chunking on strategy change.** "We moved from 256 to 512" — old vectors are still 256, the index becomes a mix, recall is inconsistent. Full re-index, not partial.

**6. Ignoring deletion.** A doc was removed at the source — its chunks stayed in the index — the user gets answers from a "ghost" doc. Tied to [[node:sys-document-pipelines|document pipelines]].

sys-hybrid-search.title: Hybrid search: sparse + dense
sys-hybrid-search.what:
Hybrid search combines two signals: **sparse** (BM25 — keyword matching, exact words, acronyms, names) and **dense** (embeddings — semantic similarity, paraphrases, concepts). Each compensates for the other's weaknesses.

Two fusion methods:

- **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)** — each method returns top-N, ranks are merged by `score = Σ 1/(k + rank_i)` with k=60. Simple, effective, no weight tuning.
- **Weighted sum** — `final_score = α × dense_score + (1-α) × sparse_score`, α≈0.5 as a starting point. Needs score normalization.

Then **rerank** the top 50-100 via a cross-encoder (Cohere Rerank, BGE-reranker) -> final top 5-10. A cross-encoder reads the query and document together — more accurate than the bi-encoder embedding, but more expensive.
sys-hybrid-search.why:
Pure dense search fails on exact terms (model names, error codes, person names), rare words (out-of-vocabulary for the embedder), and short queries. BM25 handles those — it is what Google did for 20 years before neural search.

Pure BM25 fails on paraphrases ("cancel sub" vs "subscription termination"), conceptual queries, multilingual content. Embeddings solve that.

Hybrid gains +10-25% recall@10 on typical RAG benchmarks vs dense-only.
sys-hybrid-search.when:
From day one of production RAG if you have any of:

- Technical content (names, versions, error codes, API names) — BM25 is essential
- Multilingual data
- Users who type short keyword queries ("pgvector hnsw m parameter")
- Eval recall below 80% on dense-only

Dense-only is enough when:
- Pure conversational cases, long natural-language questions
- Narrow domain where the embedder is fine-tuned
- < 10k documents (hybrid gain is small)
sys-hybrid-search.impact:
**Production setup (2026-05):**

- Vector stores with built-in hybrid: Weaviate, Qdrant (with FastEmbed), Elasticsearch + dense
- pgvector + BM25 by hand: `tsvector` for sparse + `pgvector` for dense, RRF in a SQL CTE
- Standalone BM25: Tantivy / Pyserini for self-host, OpenSearch for managed

**Reranker (optional, +5-15% precision@5):**
- Cohere Rerank: $1/1k searches, 100-200ms latency, top-tier quality
- BGE-reranker (self-host): 50-150ms on GPU, free, slightly weaker
- Feed top 50-100 to the reranker, return top 5-10

**Latency budget:** hybrid (BM25 + dense) in parallel ≈ max(times) ≈ 80-150ms; reranker adds 100-200ms. Total 200-400ms p95.

**Cost:** BM25 is cents (CPU). Dense query embedding is $0.00001/query. Rerank is $0.001/query — the reranker dominates.
sys-hybrid-search.example:
AI search over Anthropic's technical documentation (needs to catch "MCP", "Tier 3", "sonnet-4-5-20250929" and paraphrases like "how to cache a response").

```python
# Parallel: BM25 + dense
bm25_results = bm25_index.search(query, top_k=50)        # 30ms
dense_results = pgvector_search(embed(query), top_k=50)   # 50ms

# RRF fusion
def rrf(results_lists, k=60):
    scores = {}
    for results in results_lists:
        for rank, doc in enumerate(results):
            scores[doc.id] = scores.get(doc.id, 0) + 1/(k + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])

fused = rrf([bm25_results, dense_results])[:50]

# Rerank top-50 -> top-10
rerank_input = [(query, doc.text) for doc in fused]
reranked = cohere.rerank(query=query, documents=rerank_input, top_n=10)

# Return top-10 with citation metadata
return [fused[r.index] for r in reranked]
```

Dashboard: recall@10 on eval set (norm > 85%), precision@5 (after reranker, > 70%), p95 latency (< 400ms). A/B without vs with hybrid — if the gain is < 5%, chunking is probably broken, not search.
sys-hybrid-search.mistakes:
**1. Dense-only "because it is modern."** A query "sonnet-4-5-20250929 deprecation" gets paraphrased to "model retirement" and the exact match is missed. BM25 captures exact-token matches that embeddings blur.

**2. Weighted sum without normalizing scores.** BM25 scores live in 0-15, cosine similarity in 0-1 — the weighted sum is dominated by BM25. Either normalize (min-max) or use RRF (rank-based, not score-based).

**3. Reranking the whole corpus.** Cross-encoder on 1M documents = $1000+ per query. Rerank only the top 50-100 after the first stage.

**4. Using hybrid without evaluation.** You turn it on, recall does not grow, and you cannot tell why. Always have an eval set (50-200 helpful queries with ground truth) before/after, measure recall@10 and precision@5.

**5. Ignoring filters.** Hybrid without `WHERE tenant_id = X` mixes tenant data. Hybrid search and metadata filters are orthogonal — you need both.

*deprecate-watch: the reranker landscape moves fast — Cohere is the 2026-05 baseline.*

sys-document-pipelines.title: Document ingestion pipelines
sys-document-pipelines.what:
ETL for documents that feed RAG: parsing -> normalization -> deduplication -> chunking -> embedding -> write to the vector store. Not a one-off script — a continuously running pipeline with incremental sync.

Stages:

- **Source connectors** — pull from Notion, Confluence, Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, Linear, Zendesk, and so on
- **Parsing** — PDF (PyMuPDF, Unstructured), HTML (BeautifulSoup, trafilatura), Office (python-docx), Markdown
- **Normalization** — Unicode NFC, strip boilerplate (nav, footer), language detection, encoding
- **Deduplication** — full-text hash + near-dup detection (MinHash / SimHash) for versioned copies
- **Chunking** (see [[node:sys-chunking-strategies|chunking strategies]]) -> embedding -> upsert into the [[node:sys-vector-stores|vector store]]
- **Deletion handling** — webhooks or periodic diff against the source -> tombstones in the index
sys-document-pipelines.why:
Without a real pipeline, a RAG system degrades within weeks: new docs are missing, deleted docs answer like ghosts, updated docs return stale info.

A "one-shot ingestion script" works for the demo and fails in production. A real product needs incremental sync, deletion propagation, retries on flaky sources, and monitoring.
sys-document-pipelines.when:
The moment RAG ships to production. Plan the pipeline up front — "we will add it later" never happens.

Signals the pipeline is broken:
- Users see outdated information (doc updated yesterday, index a week old)
- A deleted document is still cited — privacy / compliance issue
- Duplicates in search results (the same FAQ from 3 sources)
- Recall drift over time with no clear cause
sys-document-pipelines.impact:
**Incremental sync (production baseline 2026-05):**

- **Webhook-driven** (preferred): Notion, Linear, GitHub fire events -> enqueue -> process. Source-to-index latency: 1-10 minutes.
- **Polling fallback** for sources without webhooks: cursor by `updated_at` + diff. Interval: 5min — 1h depending on volume.
- **Full re-sync**: weekly, catches missed events. Not cheap, but recovers data drift.

**Deletion strategy:**
- Soft delete (tombstone in the index + filter `is_deleted = false`) — fast, reversible
- Hard delete (DELETE from the vector store) — for GDPR / compliance, audit required

**Dedup thresholds:** exact hash match -> drop; MinHash similarity > 0.95 -> keep newer, mark as duplicate.

**Failure handling:** dead-letter queue for parse failures (corrupted PDF, encoding issue) with an alert if > 1% failure rate. Retry with exponential backoff (see [[node:sys-rate-limiting|rate limiting]]).

**Continuous ingestion cost (10k docs/day, 5k tokens avg, chunk=512):**
- Embeddings: ~$2/day (`text-embedding-3-small`)
- Compute (parse+chunk): varies, usually $5-20/day on a medium VM
sys-document-pipelines.example:
B2B SaaS, knowledge base from Confluence + Zendesk + GitHub Wiki.

```python
# Architecture: event-driven via SQS (see [[node:sys-event-driven|event-driven]])

# 1. Connectors push events
@webhook("/confluence/page-updated")
def on_confluence_update(event):
    sqs.send({"source": "confluence", "doc_id": event.page_id, "action": "upsert"})

@webhook("/zendesk/article-deleted")
def on_zendesk_delete(event):
    sqs.send({"source": "zendesk", "doc_id": event.id, "action": "delete"})

# 2. Worker processes events
def process_event(event):
    if event.action == "delete":
        vector_store.delete(filter={"source": event.source, "doc_id": event.doc_id})
        audit_log.write({"action": "delete", **event})
        return

    doc = source_client(event.source).fetch(event.doc_id)
    text = parse(doc)  # PDF/HTML/MD per type
    text = normalize(text)

    doc_hash = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()
    if doc_hash == previous_hash(event.doc_id):
        return  # no change, skip

    chunks = chunk(text, strategy=strategy_for(event.source))
    embeddings = embed_batch([c.text for c in chunks])

    # Upsert: delete old chunks for this doc, insert new
    vector_store.delete(filter={"doc_id": event.doc_id})
    vector_store.upsert([{**c, "embedding": e} for c, e in zip(chunks, embeddings)])
    save_hash(event.doc_id, doc_hash)

# 3. Dead-letter queue alarms via [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]
```

Metrics: ingestion lag (norm < 5min), parse-failure rate (< 1%), dedup rate (norm 5-15%), deletion latency.
sys-document-pipelines.mistakes:
**1. "Full re-sync every night" as the only strategy.** For 100k+ docs this is hours of compute, full re-indexing, and an outdated index 23h/day. Incremental sync + weekly full sync.

**2. Not handling deletion.** A doc removed in Confluence stays in the index, the user sees an answer linking to a 404. Webhooks on delete + periodic reconciliation are mandatory.

**3. Parsing without error handling.** One corrupted PDF breaks the whole batch and ingestion stalls. Try/except per document + dead-letter queue.

**4. No dedup.** The same FAQ is mirrored in 3 places, the user sees 3 identical hits, trust drops. Hash + MinHash dedup.

**5. Embeddings without version tracking.** You swap the embedding model and old vectors stay around — half the index on one model, half on another, results degrade. Track `embedding_model_version` in metadata + a migration plan.

**6. Pipeline without monitoring.** A connector died a week ago, no one knows, the index is frozen. Alert on ingestion lag and failure rate (see [[node:sys-monitoring|monitoring]]).

sys-supervisor-worker.title: Supervisor-worker pattern
sys-supervisor-worker.what:
